o: We must aggregate sales by season and category, then pick a single winning category per season using a three-level tie-break: highest total quantity, then highest total revenue (sum of quantity × price), then lexicographically smallest category name. The seasons are fixed buckets of months: Winter (12,1,2), Spring (3,4,5), Summer (6,7,8), Fall (9,10,11). In the example, Summer has Tech and Fitness tied at 5 units, so revenue decides ($100.00 vs $60.00), giving Tech. Since output is ordered by season ascending alphabetically (Fall, Spring, Summer, Winter), a simple ORDER BY on the season string suffices. The constraints imply we need one aggregation pass plus a per-season selection — either via a window function or a grouped join back.
k: Map each sale's month to a season with CASE or MONTH(), then GROUP BY season and category.
Rank groups within each season by total_quantity DESC, total_revenue DESC, category ASC and keep rank 1.
A self-join against a derived 'best per season' table avoids window functions if needed.

a.i: Aggregate all sales into (season, category) totals in one GROUP BY, then apply ROW_NUMBER partitioned by season and ordered by quantity DESC, revenue DESC, category ASC. Rank 1 rows are exactly the winners under the full tie-breaking rule. This is the cleanest single-pass formulation.
s: Join sales to products to get each sale's category.
Derive season from MONTH(sale_date) with a CASE expression.
GROUP BY season, category computing SUM(quantity) as total_quantity and SUM(quantity*price) as total_revenue.
Wrap in ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY season ORDER BY total_quantity DESC, total_revenue DESC, category ASC).
Filter rn = 1 and order by season ascending.

c.python:
# Database problem — submit the following MySQL query:
WITH agg AS (
  SELECT
    CASE
      WHEN MONTH(s.sale_date) IN (12,1,2) THEN 'Winter'
      WHEN MONTH(s.sale_date) IN (3,4,5) THEN 'Spring'
      WHEN MONTH(s.sale_date) IN (6,7,8) THEN 'Summer'
      ELSE 'Fall'
    END AS season,
    p.category,
    SUM(s.quantity) AS total_quantity,
    SUM(s.quantity * s.price) AS total_revenue,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
      PARTITION BY CASE
        WHEN MONTH(s.sale_date) IN (12,1,2) THEN 'Winter'
        WHEN MONTH(s.sale_date) IN (3,4,5) THEN 'Spring'
        WHEN MONTH(s.sale_date) IN (6,7,8) THEN 'Summer'
        ELSE 'Fall'
      END
      ORDER BY SUM(s.quantity) DESC, SUM(s.quantity * s.price) DESC, p.category ASC
    ) AS rn
  FROM sales s JOIN products p ON s.product_id = p.product_id
  GROUP BY season, p.category
)
SELECT season, category, total_quantity, total_revenue
FROM agg WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY season;

a.t: O(n log n) — one scan/join to aggregate n sales, then sorting groups inside each season partition for ROW_NUMBER.
a.sp: O(g) where g is the number of distinct (season, category) groups stored in the CTE.

a.i: Build the same aggregated CTE, then for each group keep only those whose (quantity, revenue, category) tuple beats every other group of the same season. Expressing this with a NOT EXISTS anti-join replicates the tie-break ordering without any ranking function.
s: Create CTE agg with season, category, total_quantity, total_revenue.
For each row r in agg, check no other row o with same season has larger quantity, equal quantity but larger revenue, or both equal but smaller category.
Use NOT EXISTS with that comparison to filter winners.

# Database problem — submit the following MySQL query:
WITH agg AS (
  SELECT
    CASE
      WHEN MONTH(s.sale_date) IN (12,1,2) THEN 'Winter'
      WHEN MONTH(s.sale_date) IN (3,4,5) THEN 'Spring'
      WHEN MONTH(s.sale_date) IN (6,7,8) THEN 'Summer'
      ELSE 'Fall'
    END AS season,
    p.category,
    SUM(s.quantity) AS total_quantity,
    SUM(s.quantity * s.price) AS total_revenue
  FROM sales s JOIN products p ON s.product_id = p.product_id
  GROUP BY season, p.category
)
SELECT a.season, a.category, a.total_quantity, a.total_revenue
FROM agg a
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM agg o
  WHERE o.season = a.season
    AND (o.total_quantity > a.total_quantity
         OR (o.total_quantity = a.total_quantity AND o.total_revenue > a.total_revenue)
         OR (o.total_quantity = a.total_quantity AND o.total_revenue = a.total_revenue AND o.category < a.category))
)
ORDER BY a.season;

a.t: O(n + g^2) — aggregation over n sales, then each of g groups is compared against up to g-1 others; fine since g ≤ 48.
a.sp: O(g) for the materialized aggregate CTE.

w: Prefer Approach 1 in an interview: it is shorter, clearly encodes the three-way tie-break in one ORDER BY, and scales better. Use Approach 2 only when window functions are unavailable. Pitfalls: forgetting December belongs to Winter (it wraps around the year), computing revenue as SUM(price) instead of SUM(quantity*price), grouping before joining to products, and ordering seasons alphabetically rather than calendar-wise — here alphabetical is required. Edge cases: ties broken twice (quantity then revenue then name), seasons with only one category, and empty seasons (they simply produce no row). Follow-ups might ask for top-k categories per season (change ROW_NUMBER to a filter on rank ≤ k), or year-aware seasons (partition by YEAR too).
